core_concepts: Centripetal acceleration always points toward the center of circular motion.
Its magnitude increases when angular velocity or linear speed increases.
Its magnitude decreases when the radius grows while other variables remain fixed.
In uniform circular motion, speed can remain constant while velocity still changes because its direction changes continuously.
Circular motion requires an inward acceleration and therefore an inward net force.

centripetal_acceleration.summary: Describes the inward acceleration required to keep an object moving in a circular path.
facts: In uniform circular motion, centripetal acceleration changes the direction of velocity, not its magnitude.
If an object moves in a circular path, an inward acceleration must exist even when speed is constant.

circular_motion.summary: Motion along a circular path with continuously changing velocity direction.
facts: Uniform circular motion means the object moves around a circle at constant speed.
Constant speed does not mean constant velocity because velocity includes direction.
Velocity and centripetal acceleration are perpendicular in uniform circular motion.

centripetal_force.summary: The inward force that causes centripetal acceleration and keeps an object moving in a circular path.
facts: Any object in uniform circular motion must experience a force toward the center.
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it can be supplied by gravity, tension, friction, or other real forces depending on the situation.

centrifugal_force.summary: An apparent outward force often discussed in rotating frames, not the real inward force that maintains circular motion.
facts: Students often confuse centripetal force with centrifugal force.
Centrifugal force should not be treated as the real physical cause that keeps an object in circular motion in an inertial frame.
The blade tip follows a circular path.
Even at constant speed, the velocity direction keeps changing.
Riders move in a circle around the center.
Larger radius changes the centripetal acceleration relationship.
Points farther from the center travel larger circular paths.
Comparing inner and outer points supports radius reasoning.
The rotating drum provides a familiar real-world example of circular motion.
Tension can act as the inward force that keeps the object moving in a circle.
A ball on a string is a classic example where centripetal force is supplied by tension.
The spinning basket rotates to remove water from vegetables.
Points on the basket follow circular paths with centripetal acceleration toward the center.
The platter rotates at constant angular velocity for uniform playback.
Points farther from the center have larger linear speed and centripetal acceleration.
An orbiting body can be modeled as circular motion with acceleration toward the center.
Gravity can provide the centripetal force for orbital motion.
A car rounding a curve requires centripetal force toward the center of the turn.
On a flat road, friction can supply the required centripetal force.
The athlete and chain provide the inward force that keeps the hammer moving in a circle.
The ball is influenced by gravity and tension, which combine to produce the net centripetal force.
For fixed speed, larger radius lowers centripetal acceleration.
For fixed angular velocity, larger radius increases centripetal acceleration.
Increasing angular velocity strongly increases centripetal acceleration.
The relationship is nonlinear because acceleration depends on omega squared.
Period can be connected to angular velocity through omega = 2pi / T.
Linear speed can be connected to period through v = 2pi r / T.
Centripetal acceleration can be connected to period through a_c = 4pi^2 r / T^2.
Period T and angular velocity omega are inversely related: omega = 2pi / T.
When period (time per revolution) increases, angular velocity decreases.
Centripetal acceleration depends on period through a_c = (2pi/T)^2 * r.
When period increases (slower rotation), centripetal acceleration decreases (inverse square).
For fixed mass and radius, centripetal force increases with the square of speed.
Doubling speed makes the required centripetal force four times larger.
For fixed mass and speed, centripetal force decreases as radius increases.
For fixed mass and period, centripetal force increases with radius.

problem_finding: Ask students to identify or find examples in their surroundings.
Avoid turning the question into a full explanation prompt.
Encourage students to distinguish between objects that merely rotate and situations where a specific point or object clearly follows a circular path.
problem_exploring: Encourage reasoning about relationships between variables or observed patterns.
A good inquiry probes one main conceptual relationship at a time.
Invite students to reason about why speed can be constant while acceleration is nonzero.
Ask students to identify what real force supplies the centripetal force in the context.
problem_generating: The generated problem must use evidence from both the graph and the image.
The final output should be a solvable physics problem, not a reflection question.
The problem may ask students to infer speed, acceleration, or force from radius and period data.

easy: Use one-step reasoning with explicit quantities.
Prefer direct substitution or identification of one relationship.
Use direct formulas such as a_c = v^2 / r or F_c = m v^2 / r.
intermediate: Ask for comparison between two conditions or moderate interpretation of data.
Combine observation from the image with one graph pattern.
Allow conversion between period and speed using v = 2pi r / T.
advanced: Allow multistep reasoning, uncertainty, or justification using more than one variable.
Expect stronger integration of graph evidence and physical interpretation.
Require identifying the source of centripetal force and separating it from misconceptions about outward force.

problem_finding: Students may confuse any spinning-looking object with true circular motion examples.
problem_exploring: Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration in circular motion.
Velocity direction and centripetal acceleration direction should not be treated as the same vector.
Students may think an outward force is required to keep an object moving in a circle.
Students may confuse centripetal force with centrifugal force.
problem_generating: The problem should not ignore one of the two visual inputs.
Avoid asking for an answer that cannot be supported by the provided graph or image.
Do not treat centripetal force as a separate physical interaction without specifying its source such as tension, gravity, or friction.

added_from_libretexts: Uniform circular motion keeps speed constant but changes velocity direction.
Centripetal acceleration formulas include a_c = v^2/r and a_c = 4pi^2 r/T^2.
Linear speed in circular motion can be written as v = 2pi r/T.
Centripetal force formulas include F_c = m v^2/r and F_c = 4pi^2 r m/T^2.
Gravity, tension, and friction can act as centripetal force depending on the context.
Centrifugal force is commonly misunderstood and should be handled as an apparent force idea, not the real inward cause in an inertial frame.
